title: A Summary of a Lecture

prepTasks.correct: Она обратила внимание на то, что...

writingModel: Summary of Professor Aidarov's Lecture on Language Change — by Kamila Seitkali

On Thursday, Professor Aidarov gave a lecture on language change. He said that language was never static and that every generation changed the language it inherited. He argued that this process was not decay but natural adaptation, and he pointed out that resistance to language change was itself a historical constant — every generation believed the next one spoke poorly.

He then moved on to the topic of language borrowing. He said that Kazakh had absorbed thousands of Russian words over the twentieth century and argued that this was not a sign of weakness but of contact between peoples. He asked us what we thought about this — he asked whether we found the idea reassuring or unsettling.

The class discussion that followed was lively. One student said she thought borrowed words were a form of cultural contamination. Another student said he believed purism was impossible because all languages had always borrowed from each other. Professor Aidarov told them both that they were partially correct. He explained that the tension between change and preservation was central to linguistics.

Professor Aidarov then told us to read Chinghiz Aitmatov. He said that Aitmatov had written in both Kazakh and Russian, and that this was not a betrayal of either language but a bridge between them. He asked us to consider what it meant to write in two languages at once.

At the end of the lecture, Professor Aidarov made an interesting observation about endangered languages. He said that large languages could disappear faster than small ones if their speakers became bilingual and stopped transmitting the language to the next generation. He concluded by saying that language survival depended not on government policy but on the daily choices of individual speakers.

Overall, the lecture was thought-provoking. Professor Aidarov encouraged us to think about language not as a fixed system but as a living practice — always in motion, always reflecting the society that uses it.

writingTemplate.hint: Introduce the lecture with when and who.
"said that" + past tense. E.g. "he said that language was never static."
"argued that" = presented an argument. Backshift the tense.
"He asked us WHETHER we agreed." / "He asked us TO CONSIDER..."
Report two different student opinions using "said that."
